method: Predictions derived from each figure's own public statements (sources listed per figure; 'src' holds indices into that list). conf: high = said almost verbatim; med = clearly implied by stated views; low = inferred from general stance. value 0-100: for 'prob' items the probability the statement is true; for 'agree' items the degree of agreement.

figures.name: Scott Alexander
figures.role: Psychiatrist and writer of the blog Astral Codex Ten (formerly Slate Star Codex); co-author of the 'AI 2027' scenario (as of Sept 2026)
figures.camp: worried forecaster, 'not as much of a doomer'
figures.bio: Psychiatrist who writes Astral Codex Ten. Co-wrote the 'AI 2027' scenario (April 2025) with Daniel Kokotajlo's AI Futures Project and helped with its July 2026 sequel, 'Plan A'. His June 2026 'My AI Opinions' gives a 20% chance AI wipes out humanity (33% in 2023), a 50% chance of AGI by 2034, and says he is 'nervously but committedly' backing pause activism. He favours a US-China deal with data-centre monitoring over a unilateral halt, and is neutral on open weights. Not on the 2023 CAIS or 2025 superintelligence lists.
figures.oneLiner: Puts doom at 20%: likelier we survive, but far too high. Wants a verified US-China slowdown, not a race and not a permanent stop.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: My AI Opinions
sources.note: His numbers in one place: AGI 25% by 2027, 50% by 2034, 75% by 2045; p(doom) 20%, plus 30% other permanent curtailment; 40% chance of a good US-China pause; 'nervously but committedly supporting' pause activism.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Introducing Plan A
sources.note: Presents the AI Futures Project's plan: 'The linchpin of Plan A is a joint AI regulatory regime with China', with audited data centres; 'When we say "we must slow down AI", we mean we want the cancer-cures-in-2035 one'.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Open Questions On Open Weights
sources.note: 'I'm also neutral about open weights AI. I think it probably won't be long-term sustainable', but would not spend political capital banning it now: 'we owe them the chance to try'.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Why AI Safety Won't Make America Lose The Race With China
sources.note: Accepts the race frame for argument's sake: safety bills (SB 53, RAISE) cost about 1% of training; export controls matter far more; most pause advocates want a mutual, treaty-based pause.

sources.title: Dwarkesh Podcast: AI 2027, with Scott Alexander and Daniel Kokotajlo (transcript)
sources.note: 'My p(doom) is the lowest of anyone on the team. I'm more like 20%'; 'not completely convinced that we don't get something like alignment by default'; only '20% chance things go as fast as our scenario says'; backs transparency rules.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: My Takeaways From AI 2027
sources.note: His own views after the scenario: hacking scares governments first; open-source lags too far to check a fast takeoff; a one-year software-only takeoff is possible; opposes campaigns for safety staff to quit labs.

sources.title: AI 2027 (scenario, co-author)
sources.note: Scenario with two endings, 'race' (misaligned AI takes over) and 'slowdown' (labs pause, keep readable chain of thought, humans keep control). Alexander is a listed co-author and did much of the writing.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate
sources.note: 'Willing to consider trying a Regulatory or Surgical Pause', strong if multilateral, otherwise 'calculated not to put us behind hostile countries'; 'if we never get AI, I expect the future to be short and grim'.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Why I Am Not (As Much Of) A Doomer (As Some People)
sources.note: 'If you force me to give an estimate it's probably around 33%'; optimistic because intermediate AIs may do alignment research before world-killers exist and because he expects gradual progress.

sources.title: CAIS: Statement on AI Risk (signatory list)
sources.note: Not a signatory: all 14 pages of the list (697 names) checked; no Scott Alexander or Siskind. Daniel Kokotajlo and Scott Aaronson are listed.

sources.title: FLI: Pause Giant AI Experiments (signatory list)
sources.note: Unverified: the full list has one 'Scott Alexander' with no affiliation, which cannot be tied to him. In Oct 2023 he called the letter 'a watered-down compromise'; he has not said he signed it.

sources.title: FLI: Statement on Superintelligence (signatory list)
sources.note: Not found: the site's signatory search returns no Scott Alexander or Siskind (Sept 2026), while Daniel Kokotajlo is listed. The statement asks for a ban until there is scientific consensus and public buy-in.

sources.title: X: Steven Pinker's post that Alexander reportedly answered with a debate challenge
sources.note: Pinker's post is verified. Alexander's reported reply of 19 Sept 2026 (a public debate with a $5,000-vs-$1,000 bet on audience opinion change) could not be retrieved or confirmed; no prediction rests on it.

sources.title: Astral Codex Ten: Mysteries Of AI Generalization
sources.note: On emergent misalignment and reward hacking: 'My best guess is that it should be very slightly reassuring, but I'm not sure'; reports a paper finding Claude 4.5 'smart enough to know that it's being tested'.

d1.basis: June 2026: 'there's a 20% chance that the first AIs to cross the point of no return will want to eliminate the human population', plus 30% other permanent curtailment. Twice the 10% bar.

d3.basis: Own odds: 25% that AGI-to-superhuman takes under a year, median 4 years; 'only like 20% chance things go as fast as our scenario says'. A sudden jump is a live risk, not his main case.

d5.basis: 50% that AI would want humans gone under 'normal corporate incentives', 20% at current safety effort; 'not completely convinced that we don't get something like alignment by default'.

d6.basis: Expects hacking and small bioterror scares first and a 50% chance of a 9/11-scale 'warning shot'; his point of no return is around 2040. No direct statement on a ten-year window.

d7.basis: Defines a 'point of no return' after which humans cannot stop AI; before it control is possible. About 80% survival and a 40% chance of a well-designed pause, but he stresses it may fail.

d9.basis: 'More optimistic about alignment than the average person who thinks about AI safety'; in his modal story the deception probes win the arms race. Still 20% doom, and experts are gloomier.

s1.basis: 'Less optimistic about a true pause/stop as opposed to a slowdown'; 'if we never get AI, I expect the future to be short and grim'. Yet a 30-year pause 'probably comes out net positive'.

s4.basis: 'A good pause strategy would involve both sides being able to monitor the other's data centers to prevent illegal training'; 'the linchpin of Plan A is a joint AI regulatory regime with China'.

s5.basis: Wants the US to keep its lead (export controls) and any unilateral pause 'calculated not to put us behind hostile countries', but backs a mutual pause and says racing is what dooms AI 2027.

s6.basis: Good pacing 'lets alignment researchers thoroughly test each generation of AIs pre-release'; backs safety cases, audits, SB 53-type bills. Long-time FDA critic; no call for a licence regime.

s8.basis: On pause risks: 'I still think it probably comes out net positive… shorter pause lengths (like five years) seem like no-brainers.'

s10.basis: Counts the costs of delay (5% each for bioweapons, nukes, decline in a 30-year pause) and still favours slowing: 'When we say "we must slow down AI", we mean… the cancer-cures-in-2035 one.'

s11.basis: 'I'm also neutral about open weights AI. I think it probably won't be long-term sustainable, but I'm happy to wait… rather than expend effort and political capital to ban it immediately.'

s13.basis: 'When we say "we must slow down AI", we mean we want the cancer-cures-in-2035 one'; on pause activism, 'I'm nervously but committedly supporting it.'

p2.basis: AGI (90% of knowledge jobs doable) 50% by 2034, 75% by 2045; diffusion gap 50% under ten years; modal: 'more than half of jobs are automated by the late 2030s'. Combined odds are my estimate.

p4.basis: 'I am worried about concentration of power, though less worried than I might otherwise be'; gaming out a corporate coup, 'I can't make it hang together'. Misalignment is his main worry.

d10.basis: His 20% p(doom), plus 30% other permanent curtailment, has no 20-year limit: AGI 50% by 2034, then 50% that the point of no return comes within 10 years. By 2046 that is roughly 10-25%.

d11.basis: June 2026: '50% chance we get a warning shot before AI crosses the point of no return'. Sept 2026: reports that Claude 4.5 is 'smart enough to know that it's being tested'.

d12.basis: 50% that the first AIs past the point of no return would want humans gone under normal corporate incentives, 20% with today's safety work; Sept 2026: new generalization results 'very slightly reassuring'.

d13.basis: June 2026: 'there's a 20% chance that the first AIs to cross the point of no return will want to eliminate the human population'. A threat to survival, not a familiar harm, is his central worry.

d14.basis: Control is possible only before a 'point of no return', after which humans could not stop a hostile AI; he gives a good US-China pause 40%. A dangerous AI is contained only if caught in time.

d15.basis: Expects hacking and small bioterror scares first, and gives a 50% chance of a 9/11- or COVID-scale scare before the point of no return; no number for millions dead. Inferred.

s14.basis: On pausing: 'I still think it probably comes out net positive… shorter pause lengths (like five years) seem like no-brainers.' A verified ten-year worldwide pause is well inside what he backs.

d16.basis: Extinction now counts: roughly 10-20% of his 20% p(doom) falls before 2046, added to hacking and bio scares short of it (d15 25). Some of his 'curtailment' is not mass death. Inferred.

s15.basis: Copied from s14. On pausing: 'shorter pause lengths (like five years) seem like no-brainers.' Plan A's pause targets frontier general AI, as s15 does.

figures.name: Steven Pinker
figures.role: Johnstone Family Professor of Psychology at Harvard University; author of Enlightenment Now and Rationality (as of Sept 2026)
figures.camp: doom sceptic: AI safety is ordinary engineering
figures.bio: Harvard cognitive psychologist and author of The Better Angels of Our Nature, Enlightenment Now (2018) and Rationality (2021). Since 2018 he has argued that AI-doom scenarios confuse intelligence with motivation and treat it as a 'miraculous elixir'; real AI hazards such as job loss, biased sorting and deception are engineering and policy problems. Debated Stuart Russell (2020) and Scott Aaronson (2022). In Sept 2026 he called the kill-us-all scenarios 'preposterous'. He signed none of the 2023 or 2025 AI-risk statements.
figures.oneLiner: The doom scenarios are 'preposterous'; being smart is not wanting power. Treat AI as normal technology: test it, fix real harms, keep going.

sources.title: X: 'Is AI really going to kill us all? The scenarios are preposterous…' (sharing Claire Lehmann in The Australian)
sources.note: Full text verified via X's embed API and his site's feed: 'The scenarios are preposterous, and the presumption of inevitability encourages fatalism, panic, and distraction from the more mundane and realistic safety challenges.'

sources.title: X: on AI leaders' 'eccentric Berkeley subculture' (sharing Cal Newport in the NYT)
sources.note: 'Why are the leaders of AI companies saying "Our products are going to extinguish humanity. Invest in us!" They come from an eccentric Berkeley subculture in which this eschatology is a sacred belief.' Rest of the long post not retrieved.

sources.title: X: looking back on his 2022 debate with Scott Aaronson
sources.note: 'I made some of these points in a debate with my friend… Scott Aaronson… (2022, before the release of ChatGPT). I underestimated what AI was about to be capable of, but expressed some of…' (post truncated by the embed API).

sources.title: X: 'AI Companies: Stop the self-serving and fatalistic doom-trolling' (sharing an NYT op-ed)
sources.note: Endorses the op-ed's line that AI is not 'some inevitable force' but 'a collection of specific tools that these companies are choosing to design and sell'. Only the first 280 characters were retrievable.

sources.title: Possible Minds (ed. Brockman): Tech Prophecy and the Underappreciated Causal Power of Ideas
sources.note: Both AI threats 'strike me as chimerical'; 'Being smart is not the same as wanting something'; the scenarios are 'self-refuting'; 'Don't build one'; AI 'is like any other technology… tested before it is implemented'; culture of safety.

sources.title: Popular Science: We're told to fear robots. But why do we think they'll turn on us? (from Enlightenment Now, ch. 19)
sources.note: The book's argument: 'foom' and AGI rest on intelligence as 'a miraculous elixir'; the mundane challenge is jobs, 'but the jobs won't be eliminated that quickly'.

sources.title: Shtetl-Optimized: Steven Pinker and I debate AI scaling!
sources.note: 'There will be no omnipotent superintelligence or wonder algorithm (or singularity or AGI or existential threat or foom), just better and better gadgets'; real dangers (unemployment, bias, deception) 'are not conjectural'.

sources.title: Richard Hanania's Newsletter: Pinker on Alignment and Intelligence as a 'Magical Potion'
sources.note: Intelligence as 'magical pixie dust'; a single-goal AI 'is not Artificial Intelligence: it's Artificial Stupidity'; building in self-preservation at all costs: 'only an idiot would do that'; AI-risk work a 'dubious allocation of intellectual capital'.

sources.title: FLI AI Alignment Podcast: Steven Pinker and Stuart Russell on the Foundations, Benefits, and Possible Existential Threat of AI
sources.note: 'Obviously, I'm in favor of the safety mindset of engineering'; existential worry risks 'stigmatization and abandonment of helpful technologies' (nuclear power, GMOs) and 'misallocating our worry budget'; jobs may need UBI.

sources.title: Harvard Gazette: Will ChatGPT supplant us as writers, thinkers?
sources.note: AGI is 'incoherent, like a "general machine"'; 'What we have now, and probably always will have, are devices that exceed humans in some challenges and not in others'; fears ignore 'the countermeasures that would arise'.

sources.note: Not a signatory: all 14 pages of the list (697 names) checked; no Pinker.

sources.title: Forbes: Who's Who In The Fight Over Whether AI Will Kill Us
sources.note: Page blocks fetchers; read only through search snippets, wording unverified. Reports Pinker telling ABC Australia that AI engineering pathogens is imaginable, but distributing them to kill everyone is 'a bit fanciful'.

d1.basis: Sept 2026: 'Is AI really going to kill us all? The scenarios are preposterous'; 2019: both takeover and value-misalignment threats 'strike me as chimerical'.

d3.basis: 'There will be no omnipotent superintelligence or wonder algorithm (or singularity or AGI or existential threat or foom), just better and better gadgets'; 'understanding does not obey Moore's Law'.

d5.basis: 'Being smart is not the same as wanting something'; goals must be 'exogenously built into a system'; the misalignment scenarios are 'self-refuting'; an all-costs drive: 'only an idiot would do that'.

d6.basis: Unemployment, invidious sorting and deception 'are not conjectural'; doom talk is a 'distraction from the more mundane and realistic safety challenges' (Sept 2026).

d7.basis: A power-seeking AI 'without the cooperation of humans… would remain an impotent brain in a vat'; for a Doomsday Computer, 'Don't build one'; off switches and fuses are 'just engineering'.

d9.basis: AI 'is like any other technology… developed incrementally… tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety'; cites a 95% fall in accident deaths. He rejects the smarter-than-us premise.

s1.basis: Never asked directly, but he denies the premise: doom fears bring 'stigmatization and abandonment of helpful technologies', like nuclear power; AI-risk work is a 'dubious allocation of intellectual capital'.

s4.basis: No statement on an AI treaty found. He sees the threat as chimerical, so a nuclear-style inspection regime would have nothing to guard against. Inferred from general stance.

s5.basis: No stated view on AI geopolitics found. He rejects treating AI as 'some inevitable force' and is no race hawk, but sees no reason to hold back either. Placed at the midpoint.

s6.basis: 'Test the living daylights out of any system before we give it control over anything' and praises safety regulation, but calls GMOs 'overregulated… out of worst-case fears'. No view on licensing found.

s8.basis: Sees the catastrophe risk as negligible, so delay buys nothing, and says worst-case fear has real costs: 'What's catastrophic is that we don't roll out nuclear power the way that France did.'

s10.basis: 'There are tremendous potential benefits to AI… we ought to seek at the same time as we anticipate the reasonable risks'; the nuclear-power and GMO analogies put the cost on excess caution.

s11.basis: No statement on open weights found. Civil-libertarian instincts point one way; his view that the real hazard is what people do with the tools points the other. Placed at the midpoint.

s13.basis: Opposes slowing out of doom fears, but never says 'as fast as we can': he wants testing, a safety culture and regulation that learns from accidents. Inferred from general stance.

p2.basis: 2018: 'the jobs won't be eliminated that quickly'; 2023: 'probably always' tools that beat humans at some tasks only. But July 2026: 'I underestimated what AI was about to be capable of.'

p4.basis: Endorses Wiener: 'the machine's danger to society is not from the machine itself but from what man makes of it'; 'it's the norms and laws we should be vigilant about, not the tech'.

d10.basis: Sept 2026: 'Is AI really going to kill us all? The scenarios are preposterous'; 2019: both takeover and value-misalignment threats 'strike me as chimerical'.

d11.basis: AI 'is like any other technology… developed incrementally… tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety'. Problems show up and get fixed along the way.

d12.basis: 'Being smart is not the same as wanting something'; goals must be 'exogenously built into a system'; the misalignment scenarios are 'self-refuting'.

d13.basis: Unemployment, invidious sorting and deception 'are not conjectural'; doom talk is a 'distraction from the more mundane and realistic safety challenges' (Sept 2026).

d14.basis: A power-seeking AI 'without the cooperation of humans… would remain an impotent brain in a vat'; for a Doomsday Computer, 'Don't build one'; off switches and fuses are 'just engineering'.

d15.basis: Reported (ABC via Forbes, unverified): AI-engineered pathogens are imaginable, killing everyone 'a bit fanciful'. He treats real hazards as mundane and manageable. No view on millions dead found.

s14.basis: Would not press: doom fears bring 'stigmatization and abandonment of helpful technologies', as with nuclear power. He sees no danger a ten-year freeze would avert. Inferred.

d16.basis: Copied from d15. Calls doom scenarios 'preposterous', so dropping the clause adds nothing; treats real hazards as mundane and manageable. No view on millions dead found.

s15.basis: Copied from s14. He sees no danger a freeze would avert and warns that doom fears lead to abandoning helpful technology; the narrowing does not change that. Inferred.
